# Abstract

Chechnya and Ingushetia occupy 20,8k km² on the northern flank of the Greater Caucasus (17,2k km² in the Chechen Republic and 3,6k km² in the Republic of Ingushetia). Across the last twelve millennia, settlement in the region has shifted repeatedly between the fertile piedmont plains of the Sunzha, Assa and Argun rivers and the defensive limestone gorges of the high mountains. Early Holocene canyon camps and Early Bronze Age villages at Lugovoye, Bamut and Serzhen-Yurt I, where the Kura-Araxes and Maykop traditions met, raised the regional population to around 18k by 3000BC [@munchaev1961lugovoye; @munchaev1975caucasus; @bagaev2008ancient]. During the Late Bronze and Early Iron Ages (1200-400BC), fortified hillforts and bronze-working centres of the Eastern Koban culture at Serzhen-Yurt, Zandak and Nesterovskiy supported 56k inhabitants by 1000BC and 78k by 500BC [@kozenkova1977koban; @kozenkova1992serzhen; @kozenkova2013koban; @burkov2015]. Population reached a medieval peak of 172k (145k-200k) around 1200AD under the Alanic kingdom, when three-quarters of the inhabitants lived on the piedmont plain around the walled urban centres of Alkhan-Kala (60 ha), Germenchuk and the Magas settlement cluster around Nazran and Ekazhevo [@vinogradov1972central; @chakhkiev2006magas; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @malashev2016alania; @mamaev2009]. The Mongol siege of Magas in 1239-1240 and Timur's campaign against Simsir in 1395 destroyed the lowland towns, halving the regional population to 88k (75k-105k) by 1400AD and driving 77% of the survivors into the fortified stone tower villages of the Armkhi, Assa and Argun gorges, including Egikal, Erzi, Targim, Vovnushki, Tsoy-Pede and Khoy [@markovin1965monuments; @shavkhelishvili1963history; @akhmadov2002chechnya; @frizen2020]. From the 16th to the 18th century, Vainakh communities descended once more onto the Sunzha-Argun plains, lifting numbers to 128k by 1700AD and 220k by 1800AD [@kusheva1963peoples; @volkova1973ethnonyms; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @kabuzan1996]. Although the Caucasian War (1818-1859) reduced the population to 195k in 1850AD and was followed in 1865 by the *muhajir* emigration of some 22k Chechens and Orstkhoy to the Ottoman Empire, agrarian recovery, Cossack colonisation and the Grozny oil boom of the 1890s carried the population to 350k (330k-370k) by 1900AD [@kabuzan1996; @ibragimova2006; @troynitskiy1905terek; @golovlev2017census].

# Background

Occupying the north-central and north-eastern slopes of the Greater Caucasus between the upper Terek-Assa watershed and the Andi ridge, the historical Vainakh territory (20,8k km²) divides naturally into three parallel east-west belts (Figure 1 and Table 1).

At the foot of the mountains lies the Sunzha-Assa-Argun piedmont plain and its adjoining foothill valleys (Zone 1, 8,6k km², 100-500 m). Watered by the Sunzha and its right-bank tributaries - the Assa, Fortanga, Gehi, Martan, Argun, Dzhalka, Gums and Aksay - this fertile belt served as the primary agricultural heartland of the region during the Early Bronze Age (Lugovoye, Serzhen-Yurt I), the Eastern Koban period (Serzhen-Yurt, Alkhaste, Bamut), the Alanic kingdom (Alkhan-Kala, Nazran-Ekazhevo/Magas) and the 16th-19th-century Vainakh resettlement of the plains (Chechen-Aul, Aldy, Shali, Germenchuk, Gekhi, Urus-Martan, Nazran and Grozny) [@munchaev1961lugovoye; @kozenkova1992serzhen; @chakhkiev2006magas; @akhmadov2002chechnya].

South of the piedmont rise the limestone and slate tower gorges of the high mountains (Zone 2, 6,7k km², 500-4.493 m). Culminating in Mount Tebulosmta (4.493 m) and Mount Shan (4.451 m), the deep canyons of the Armkhi (Dzheirakh), upper Assa (Targim basin), Fortanga (Orstkhoy/Akki), upper Argun (Malkhista, Maysta, Terloy, Chanti, Shubuty and Mulkoi), Sharo-Argun (Sharoy and Cheberloy) and wooded Ichkeria (Nokhch-Mokhk) formed natural mountain refuges [@markovin1965monuments; @chakhkiev2007weapons; @nalgiev2026]. Following the 13th- and 14th-century Mongol and Timurid campaigns across the Sunzha plain, these gorges saw extensive construction of mortar-bound residential stone towers (*gala*), pyramidal combat towers (*vov*) and above-ground collective vaulted crypts (*maigash* or *kash*) [@markovin1965monuments; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @karieva2024].

North of the Terek river extends the Trans-Terek lowland steppe (Zone 3, 5,5k km², -10 to 150 m). Across the Naurskaya, Shelkovskaya and Kargalinskaya steppes, mobile pastoralists - Scythians, Sarmatians, Savirs, Khazars, Kipchaks, Golden Horde Tatars and Nogais - alternated with fortified river settlements along the Terek bluff and, from the 16th to the 19th century, the Greben and Terek Cossack *stanitsas* [@vinogradov1972central; @kusheva1963peoples; @kabuzan1996].

# Methodology

## Regional Subdivisions

To track population movements between the fertile Sunzha-Assa-Argun piedmont and the mountain gorges, we divide Chechnya and Ingushetia (20,8k km²) into three elevation zones (Table 1).

## Estimation Methods

Our population estimates combine archaeological settlement and cemetery surveys for the prehistoric and medieval eras with Russian diplomatic, military and census records from the 16th century onwards.

For the Eastern Koban period (1200-400BC), V. I. Kozenkova's excavations at Serzhen-Yurt I-II - an 8-10 ha craft settlement with cobbled streets, more than 60 timber-and-wattle dwellings and bronze-foundry workshops, paired with an adjacent cemetery of over 120 flat graves - together with surveys at Zandak, Bamut, Nesterovskiy and Lugovoye indicate densities of 40-65 persons per hectare, or 400-650 residents per major hillfort [@kozenkova1977koban; @kozenkova1992serzhen; @kozenkova2013koban; @burkov2015].

For the Alanic period (400-1238AD), mapped by V. B. Vinogradov, Kh. M. Mamaev, D. Yu. Chakhkiev and V. Yu. Malashev [@burkov2007; @mamaev2009], urban and rural populations are derived from walled fort areas (80-120 persons/ha) and open farming suburbs (*posady*, 25-40 persons/ha). The largest concentrations stood at Alkhan-Kala, where a 60 ha fortified core and over 150 ha of suburbs housed 8k-15k inhabitants, and in the Nazran-Ekazhevo and Ali-Yurt (Magas) cluster, where more than 30 fortified towns across 100 km² supported 15k-25k inhabitants [@chakhkiev2006magas; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @malashev2016alania; @mamaev2022early].

During the late medieval highland refuge phase (1300-1700AD) in Zone 2, over 300 fortified stone tower villages (*aul-kreposti*) containing more than 2k residential towers (*gala*, two to three storeys housing a family of 5,5-6,5 persons) and over 250 pyramidal combat towers (*vov*, four to six storeys, 22-31 m high) provide a direct house count. These figures are checked against skeleton counts inside multi-tiered collective stone crypts at Tsoy-Pede (42 crypts), Egikal, Erzi, Khoy and Vaserkel, where each family crypt accumulated 60-150 burials across six to eight generations [@markovin1965monuments; @chakhkiev2007weapons; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @frizen2020; @nalgiev2026].

From 1550 to 1800AD, Russian ambassadorial (*Posolskiy Prikaz*) and fortress registers compiled by E. N. Kusheva [@kusheva1963peoples], N. G. Volkova [@volkova1973ethnonyms; @volkova1974ethnic] and Ya. Z. and Sh. B. Akhmadov [@akhmadov2004; @akhmadov2016; @tovsultanov2017] record village counts (*kabaki* or *auly*), household totals (*dvory*) and military levies across *Okotskaya zemlya* (Aukh), *Michkizskaya zemlya* (Ichkeria), *Shubutskaya zemlya* (Shatoy/Argun), *Kalkanskaya* and *Erokanskaya zemlya* (the Ingush gorges) and the resettled Sunzha-Argun plains [@akhmadov2002chechnya; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @akhmadov2020taip]. Late 19th-century figures (1860-1900AD) are anchored to A. P. Berger's 1859 village enumerations [@berger1859chechnya], the 1867-1890 statistical tables of Terek Oblast analysed by Z. Kh. Ibragimova [@ibragimova2006] and V. M. Kabuzan [@kabuzan1996], the 1886 family lists (*posemeynye spiski*) and the 1897 imperial census returns for the Grozny, Vedeno, Nazran/Sunzha and left-bank Terek Cossack districts [@troynitskiy1905terek; @golovlev2017census].

## Mesolithic to Early and Middle Bronze Ages: Kezenoy-Am, Lugovoye and Bamut

During the Early Holocene (10000-5000BC), Mesolithic and Neolithic hunter-gatherers occupied high-mountain lake basins such as Kezenoy-Am (1.870 m) and limestone cave overhangs in the Argun, Sharoy and Assa gorges, with numbers rising gradually from 0,5k in 10000BC to 3,8k in 5000BC [@munchaev1975caucasus; @bagaev2008ancient]. In the 4th and 3rd millennia BC (4000-2000BC), the Sunzha-Assa-Argun piedmont became an active contact zone between the North-Eastern Caucasian Kura-Araxes culture and the Maykop-Novosvobodnaya kurgan tradition [@munchaev1961lugovoye; @munchaev1975caucasus].

Excavations by R. M. Munchaev (1952-1957) at Lugovoye (Muzhichi) in the Assa gorge of Ingushetia, which included 157 burials, and in the lower layer of Serzhen-Yurt I in the Shali district of Chechnya uncovered wattle-and-daub houses with sunken circular hearths, horn-lugged Kura-Araxes burnished pottery, stone shaft-hole axes and arsenical bronze daggers and spiral temple rings [@munchaev1961lugovoye; @munchaev1975caucasus]. On the Fortanga-Assa piedmont exit at Bamut, Munchaev excavated over 50 Early and Middle Bronze Age kurgans combining Maykop-Novosvobodnaya metalwork with Kura-Araxes domestic pottery [@munchaev1975caucasus]. By 3000BC, piedmont farming villages and transhumant herders numbered 18k (14k-24k), growing under the Middle Bronze Age North Caucasian (Ginchi and Pre-Koban) cultures at Galaity, Achkhoy-Martan and Harachoy to 26k in 2000BC and 36k in 1500BC [@bagaev2008ancient].

## Late Bronze and Early Iron Ages: The Eastern Koban Hillforts

Between the 12th and 5th centuries BC, Chechnya and Ingushetia formed the core territory of the Eastern Koban culture, investigated in detail by V. I. Kozenkova and M. Kh. Bagaev [@kozenkova1977koban; @kozenkova1992serzhen; @kozenkova2013koban; @bagaev2008ancient; @burkov2015; @spasskaya2024].

Situated on two naturally defended river terraces above the Bass river in the Shali district, Serzhen-Yurt I-II functioned from the 11th to the 6th century BC as a major craft and farming centre of 8-10 ha. Excavations revealed cobble-paved streets 4 m wide, rows of timber-framed clay dwellings (20-45 m²), bronze-smelting furnaces with clay tuyères and stone casting moulds for Koban shaft-hole axes, zoomorphic terracotta figurines and grain storage pits [@kozenkova1992serzhen; @kozenkova2001; @kozenkova2013koban].

More than 80 Eastern Koban settlements and cemeteries line the Sunzha-Assa-Argun foothills and mountain gorges, including the Zandak stone-cist cemetery in Nozhay-Yurt (over 60 graves) as well as Nesterovskiy, Alkhaste, Lugovoye and Sharoy, which yielded bimetallic iron-and-bronze daggers and early Scythian *akinakes* weapons from the 7th to 5th centuries BC [@kozenkova1977koban; @bagaev2008ancient]. Supported by mixed millet and barley cultivation and mountain sheep and cattle husbandry, with terraced fields covering 5,9% of mountainous Ingushetia [@shaev2024terraces], the regional population rose from 56k (45k-70k) in 1000BC to 78k (65k-95k) in 500BC.

## Sarmatian and Alanic Towns: *Magas* and *Alkhan-Kala*

During the Sarmatian period (300BC - 300AD, reaching 95k at 1AD) and the Early Alanic period (400-800AD, rising from 110k in 400AD to 140k in 800AD), a dense network of earthen-rampart and moated fortified towns (*gorodishcha*) grew up along the Sunzha, Assa, Argun and Terek rivers [@vinogradov1970; @vinogradov1972central; @malashev2016; @malashev2016alania; @mamaev2009; @burkov2007].

Protected by triple concentric horseshoe ramparts and deep moats backing onto a steep cliff above the Sunzha 18 km west of Grozny, Alkhan-Kala enclosed a 60 ha urban core surrounded by more than 150 ha of craft suburbs and a vast catacomb cemetery of over 2,5k kurgan and flat burials spanning the 2nd to 12th centuries AD [@vinogradov1970; @vinogradov1972central; @malashev2016; @mamaev2009]. As the main administrative and trading centre of the central Sunzha basin, Alkhan-Kala housed 8k-15k inhabitants before its destruction in 1238-1240.

In the upper Sunzha, Assa and Kambileyevka plains of lowland Ingushetia, surveys by D. Yu. Chakhkiev, N. D. Kodzoev and U. B. Gadiev mapped the Nazran-Ekazhevo-Yandare cluster of over 30 fortified *gorodishcha* and more than 60 satellite villages spaced 0,5-2 km apart within a 100 km² core, including Hatrig-Yurt, Ekazhevo I-IV, Nazran, Ali-Yurt, Surkhakhi, Yandare and Gazi-Yurt [@chakhkiev2003; @chakhkiev2006magas; @kodzoev2002; @gadiev2015; @dolgieva2013ingushetia]. Identified by regional archaeologists with the Alanic capital Magas (*Ma'as*, described by al-Mas'udi in 943AD and besieged by the Mongol princes Möngke, Güyük, Kadan and Büri from winter 1239 to early 1240 according to Juwayni and Rashid al-Din), this urban cluster housed 15k-25k inhabitants [@chakhkiev2006magas; @dolgieva2013ingushetia].

Further east along the Sunzha and Argun, fortified towns at Germenchuk, Shali, Aldy and Goryacheistochnenskoye (15-45 ha each) controlled the Argun-Sunzha confluence and the Terek crossings [@mamaev1979; @mamaev2009]. At its pre-Mongol peak around 1200AD, Chechnya and Ingushetia supported 172k (145k-200k) inhabitants (8,27 persons/km²), with 75% (129k) living on the Sunzha-Assa-Argun piedmont plain (Zone 1).

## Mongol and Timurid Invasions and the Highland Stone Tower Villages

Between 1238 and 1395AD, two waves of invasion destroyed the lowland towns and villages of Chechnya and Ingushetia (Figure 2B and Figure 3).

Following the storming of Magas (1239-1240), Alkhan-Kala and Dedyakov (besieged by a joint Mongol and Rus' force in 1277-1278), the fertile Sunzha and Terek plains were turned into winter pastures (*kochev'ya*) of the Golden Horde khans Batu, Berke and Uzbek; Ibn Battuta visited Uzbek Khan's camp at *Bish-Dag* in 1334 [@dolgieva2013ingushetia; @akhmadov2002chechnya]. Total regional population fell by nearly 40% to 105k (85k-125k) by 1300AD.

After defeating Tokhtamysh on the Terek in April 1395, Timur invaded the Vainakh principality of Simsir, ruled by Gayur Khan across Ichkeria and the Sunzha-Argun foothills, and marched into the highland gorges (*Aukhar*, *Buri-Burd*, *Kuli* and *Taus*). As recorded by Sharaf al-Din Yazdi and Nizam al-Din Shami, Timur's troops demolished stone fortresses, burned terraced fields and slaughtered defenders across the mountains [@shavkhelishvili1963history; @akhmadov2002chechnya]. By 1400AD, the regional population dropped to a late medieval low of 88k (75k-105k) and shifted sharply into the uplands: 77% (67,8k) of all inhabitants were now concentrated in the mountain gorges of Zone 2, leaving only 18% (15,8k) on the Sunzha plain (Zone 1).

Refugee movement into the limestone canyons of the Armkhi (Dzheirakh), upper Assa (Targim basin), Fortanga and upper Argun (Malkhista, Maysta, Terloy, Chanti and Cheberloy) spurred the construction of Vainakh stone tower complexes from the 14th to the 17th century, documented by V. I. Markovin and D. Yu. Chakhkiev (Figure 4B) [@markovin1965monuments; @chakhkiev2007weapons; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @nalgiev2026].

Among the Ingush gorges of the Targim basin and Armkhi valley (Egikal, Erzi, Targim, Khamkhi, Vovnushki and Puy), Egikal alone contained over 50 mortar-bound residential stone towers (*gala*), five intact pyramidal combat towers (*vov*, up to 27 m high with machicolations and slate-slab roofs), six subterranean and 106 above-ground collective stone crypts (*kash*) and three sanctuary shrines, including Tkhaba-Yerdy and Albi-Yerdy [@markovin1965monuments; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @karieva2024]. At the confluence of the Chanty-Argun and Meshi-Khi rivers in Malkhista, the Chechen necropolis of Tsoy-Pede preserved 42 gabled stone collective crypts guarded by two defensive barrier walls and combat towers, accumulating more than 3k burials between the 14th and 17th centuries [@markovin1965monuments; @frizen2020]. In Cheberloy (Kezenoy-Am basin), the cliff settlement of Khoy and the seven-tower complex of Sharoy anchored dense terraced mountain communities alongside Nikaroy, Vaserkel and Pakoch [@chakhkiev2007weapons; @ilyasov2004].

## Return to the Plains: Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Vainakh Societies

Following the breakup of the Golden Horde and the founding of the Russian fortress of Terki (1567/1588) on the lower Terek, land scarcity on the mountain terraces of Zone 2 prompted a gradual Vainakh return to the forested foothills (*Chernye gory*) and the Sunzha-Argun-Aksay plains between 1550 and 1700AD [@kusheva1963peoples; @volkova1973ethnonyms; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @akhmadov2020taip; @albogachiev2025].

Russian *Posolskiy Prikaz* ambassadorial journals (Semen Zvenigorodskiy in 1589, Fedor Takmakov in 1604, Khodotetskiy in 1638 and the Terki Voivode Books of 1614-1690) analysed by E. N. Kusheva [@kusheva1963peoples], N. G. Volkova [@volkova1973ethnonyms; @volkova1974ethnic] and Ya. Z. Akhmadov [@akhmadov2002chechnya; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @akhmadov2020taip; @tovsultanov2017] indicate that the total population of Chechnya and Ingushetia grew from 98k in 1500AD to 112k in 1600AD and 128k (110k-145k) by 1700AD (Figure 4A and Table 2).

In the eastern foothills, *Okotskaya zemlya* (Aukh) along the Aksay, Yamansu and Aktash rivers (Staryy Okokh and Shovkhal-Berd) was ruled by the mirzas Shikh-Murza (killed in 1596) and Batay-Murza, who fielded 500-1k horsemen and footmen in Russian service, corresponding to roughly 850 households or 5,5k inhabitants alongside the *Okotskaya sloboda* at Terki [@kusheva1963peoples; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @albogachiev2025]. *Michkizskaya zemlya* (wooded Ichkeria or Nokhch-Mokhk) comprised 36 large villages along the Michik, Gums, Hulhulau and Aksay rivers (Benoy, Tsontaroy, Gordali, Alleroy, Zandak and Vedeno), where *Posolskiy Prikaz* reports of 1619-1647 credit the *Michkizy* with 3k-5k fighting men, or 3,8k-4,6k households and 24k-30k inhabitants [@kusheva1963peoples; @akhmadov2019chechnya].

In the upper and middle Argun societies (Shubuty/Shatoy, Chanti, Mulkoi, Terloy, Malkhista, Maysta and Peshkhoy) controlling the gorge route to Tusheti and Khevsureti, the population reached 3,6k-4,4k households (21k-26k inhabitants) [@akhmadov2019chechnya; @akhmadov2020taip; @akhmadov2004], while Cheberloy and Sharoy supported 2k-2,5k households (12k-15k inhabitants) [@akhmadov2019chechnya].

To the west, the Ingush mountain societies (Kalkanskaya/Galgai, Erokanskaya/Dzheirakh, Khamkhi and Fyappiy/Metskhal) and early plains settlements in the Angusht and Tarskaya valley numbered 2,2k-2,8k households (13k-17k inhabitants) [@dolgieva2013ingushetia; @volkova1974ethnic], while the Karabulaki (Orstkhoy on the Fortanga-Assa) and Akki (Akkintsy/Galashki) numbered 1,6k-2,1k households (9,5k-13k inhabitants) [@volkova1974ethnic; @akhmadov2019chechnya; @albogachiev2025]. Over the second half of the 17th century, new flatland Chechen *auls* on the Sunzha and lower Argun (Chechen-Aul, Staraya Sunzha, Shali, Germenchuk, Aldy, Gekhi and Atterki) expanded rapidly to 3,8k-4,6k households (22k-29k inhabitants), lifting the piedmont share (Zone 1) back to 45% by 1700AD [@akhmadov2002chechnya; @akhmadov2020taip].

## The Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries

The 18th and 19th centuries brought the completion of Vainakh lowland settlement across the Sunzha-Grozny plains, the construction of the Russian Terek-Sunzha fortified line, heavy wartime losses during the Caucasian War (1818-1859) and rapid demographic growth after 1865 [@akhmadov2002history19c; @kabuzan1996; @ibragimova2006; @dolgieva2013ingushetia].

Throughout the 18th century, Chechen and Ingush settlers founded large agricultural villages of 1k-3,5k inhabitants across Greater and Lesser Chechnya (Shali, Germenchuk, Urus-Martan, Goyty, Gekhi, Achkhoy, Gudermes, Avtury and Mayrtup) and the Nazran-Kambileyevka plain (Angusht, Sholkhi and Nazran, where Ingush elders swore allegiance to Russia in 1770 and 1810) [@akhmadov2002history19c; @akhmadov2016; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @zhurtova2014]. Over the same period, the Russian Empire built the Terek-Mozdok Cordon Line along the left bank of the Terek (Kizlyar in 1735, Mozdok in 1763 and Vladikavkaz in 1784), settling Greben, Terek-Semeynye and Volga Cossacks across the Naurskaya and Shelkovskaya steppes (Zone 3) [@kabuzan1996]. The combined Vainakh and Cossack population rose from 128k in 1700AD to 165k (145k-185k) in 1750AD and 220k (190k-250k) in 1800AD, with 62% (136,5k) living on the Sunzha-Argun piedmont plains [@kabuzan1996; @akhmadov2002history19c].

General A. P. Yermolov's construction of the Sunzha Fortified Line, anchored by the fortress of Groznaya (founded in 1818), and the eviction of Chechen villages between the Terek and Sunzha rivers ignited the 1818-1859 war, during which Chechnya served as the main agricultural and military base of Imam Shamil's Caucasian Imamate (with capitals at Dargo in 1840-1845 and Vedeno in 1845-1859) [@kabuzan1996; @ibragimova2006]. Repeated military campaigns, forest-clearing (*proseki*), winter blockades of lowland pastures and the replacement of Orstkhoy (Karabulak) and western Chechen foothill villages with the Sunzha Cossack Line (the *stanitsas* of Sleptsovskaya, Troitskaya, Karabulakskaya, Assinskaya, Samashkinskaya and Mikhailovskaya in 1845-1860) inflicted severe population losses. Russian military-statistical estimates summarised by A. P. Berger [@berger1859chechnya], V. M. Kabuzan [@kabuzan1996] and Z. Kh. Ibragimova [@ibragimova2006] indicate that ethnic Chechen numbers dropped from 250k-300k in the 1830s to 130k-150k by 1859-1860, giving a regional midpoint of 195k (170k-220k) across Chechnya and Ingushetia including Cossack settlements in 1850AD. In the summer of 1865, imperial authorities organised the *muhajir* emigration of 22k-23k Chechens and nearly the entire Orstkhoy population (around 5k families) to the Ottoman Empire [@ibragimova2006; @kabuzan1996; @dolgieva2013ingushetia].

Between 1866 and 1900, agrarian recovery on the Sunzha-Argun maize and wheat plains, the 1886 family lists (recording roughly 195k ethnic Chechens and 38k Ingush) and the discovery of the Grozny oilfield in 1893 alongside the Vladikavkaz Railway drove rapid expansion [@ibragimova2006; @kabuzan1996]. In the First General Census of the Russian Empire (28 January 1897) for Terek Oblast [@troynitskiy1905terek; @golovlev2017census], native Vainakh speakers across the oblast numbered 274k (226,5k Chechens and 47,5k Ingush). Within the districts corresponding to modern Chechnya and Ingushetia - the Grozny Okrug (226k inhabitants, including 15,6k in Grozny city), the Sunzha (Nazran) Otdel (around 47,4k Ingush and 36k Sunzha Cossacks), the Chechen sector of the Khasavyurt Okrug (around 18,1k Aukh Chechens) and the left-bank Kizlyar and Mozdok Terek Cossack *stanitsas* (Naurskaya, Shelkovskaya, Chervlennaya and Kalinovskaya, totalling around 40k inhabitants) - the population reached 350k (330k-370k, or 16,83 persons/km²) by 1900AD. Of these inhabitants, 68% (238k) lived on the Sunzha-Assa-Argun plains and in the Grozny urban district (Zone 1), 18% (63k) in the mountain gorges (Zone 2) and 14% (49k) across the Trans-Terek Cossack steppe (Zone 3) [@troynitskiy1905terek; @ibragimova2006; @kabuzan1996].

# Limitations

Two main problems affect historical population estimates for Chechnya and Ingushetia. First, because family crypts (*kash* or *maigash*) at Tsoy-Pede, Egikal and Erzi stayed in continuous use from the 14th to the 18th century, until Islamisation replaced crypt burial with underground *keschnash* cemeteries, skeleton counts have to be divided by six to eight generations (180-240 years) to estimate the living population in any single century [@markovin1965monuments; @dolgieva2013ingushetia; @frizen2020]. Second, during the Caucasian War and the repeated boundary changes in Terek Oblast between 1860 and 1905 (which merged and split the Grozny, Vedeno, Ichkeria, Argun and Sunzha/Nazran districts), military estimates of unpacified mountain villages carried wider margins of error (15-20%) prior to the 1886 family lists and the 1897 census [@ibragimova2006; @kabuzan1996].

# Conclusion

The population history of Chechnya and Ingushetia from 10000BC to 1900AD was shaped by a recurring movement between the fertile Sunzha-Argun plains and the stone gorges of the Greater Caucasus. After reaching two early lowland peaks during the Eastern Koban period (78k in 500BC) and the Alanic urban era around Magas and Alkhan-Kala (172k in 1200AD), the population retreated into the mountain gorges following the Mongol and Timurid invasions, which reduced regional numbers to 88k in 1400AD and concentrated 77% of the survivors in the uplands. Subsequent Vainakh resettlement of the plains lifted the population to 128k by 1700AD and 220k by 1800AD. Despite heavy losses during the Caucasian War and the 1865 *muhajir* deportations, agrarian recovery, Cossack settlement and the Grozny oil boom carried the regional population to 350k (16,83 persons/km²) by 1900AD.
